title: The Main Story: AI Data Centers Are Plugged Into Your Electric Bill
dek: A grid auction that keeps hitting its price cap, utilities that earn more the more they build, and tech giants with tax breaks and NDAs. Whoever orders the power should pay for it.
body:
## Your toaster has a new roommate

Let's talk about your electric bill. Not the fun part of your electric bill, because there isn't one. The other part: the part that keeps going up.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration expects the average American household to pay 18.2 cents a kilowatt-hour for electricity this year, up from 17.3 cents in 2025, and 18.7 cents next year [11]. Residential prices already rose 7.1 percent in 2025, more than double the rate of inflation, and some states topped 20 percent [5]. One man in Manassas, Virginia, told Consumer Reports his January bill hit $281, up from about $100 the month before, and said it was "so far beyond any bill that I've ever had" [5].

There are a lot of reasons power gets expensive: aging wires, extreme weather, fuel prices [4]. But tonight we're going to talk about one specific machine, because it's very large, very hungry and, in a lot of the country, eating off your plate. That machine is the AI data center, and the system that decides who pays for feeding it was built for a world where electricity demand grew about as fast as a houseplant.

## How a grid auction became a ransom note

Most of the mid-Atlantic and Midwest gets its power through PJM Interconnection, the grid operator for all or parts of 13 states plus Washington, D.C. [3]. Every year PJM holds an auction to buy "capacity," which is a promise from power plants to be available years from now, and the cost of those promises lands on everyone's bill [3].

For the 2024/25 delivery year, capacity cost $28.92 per megawatt-day in most of PJM [3]. The next year it was $269.92 [3]. The year after that, $329.17, and it would have gone higher if a price cap hadn't stopped it [3]. Then, last December, the auction for 2027/28 cleared at $333.44, which was exactly the cap, for a total bill of about $16.4 billion [1]. When your price lands on the legal maximum three times in a row, that's not a market. That's a vending machine that only has one button and the button says "everything."

And here's the part PJM said out loud. Its forecast of peak demand rose by about 5,250 megawatts from one auction to the next, and nearly 5,100 of those megawatts came from data centers [1]. Even at the capped price, the auction came up 6,623 megawatts short of what PJM says it needs to keep the lights on, leaving a reserve margin of 14.8 percent against a 20 percent target [1]. As PJM's own market executive Stu Bresler put it, "data centers' demand for electricity continues to far outstrip new supply" [1]. So we paid record prices and still didn't get enough. That's like tipping 40 percent at a restaurant that forgot to bring the food.

## The receipt, itemized

PJM has an independent market monitor, Monitoring Analytics, whose whole job is to check the math. Its math is rough. The monitor estimates that existing and forecast data center load raised capacity costs for everyone else by about $9.3 billion in the 2025/26 auction, $7.3 billion in 2026/27, and $6.5 billion in 2027/28 [2]. Add it up and that's $23.1 billion over three auctions [2]. Remember that number. It'll be back.

The monitor also says the price cap is the only reason the latest figure isn't worse: with the original rules, data center load would have raised 2027/28 capacity revenue by about $19.4 billion [2]. So the good news is that the cap worked. The bad news is that "it could've been $19 billion" is now what passes for good news.

What does that look like on an actual bill? An analysis by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis found that residential Pepco bills in Washington, D.C., rose about $21 a month starting in June 2025, with roughly $10 of that from capacity prices [3]. Capacity prices added about $18 a month in western Maryland and $16 in Ohio [3]. Nobody in western Maryland asked a chatbot to write their wedding toast. They're paying for it anyway.

And the forecasts driving all this keep ballooning. In 2022, the forecast for northern Virginia's Dominion zone called for about 5,700 megawatts of growth by 2037; by 2025, the forecast was more than 20,000 megawatts of growth from data centers alone [3]. IEEFA warned that those forecasts may be inflated, but the market is already pricing them in [3]. Which means you can now pay for a data center that might not get built. That's not a utility bill, that's a Kickstarter.

## Who wins

Here's how the money moves. Investor-owned utilities earn an authorized return on what they invest, and that return averages about 9.84 percent, according to S&P Global figures cited by the utility watchdog PowerLines [10]. Build more substations and transmission lines, and there's more to earn a return on. In the third quarter of this year, utilities filed a record $4.5 billion in rate increase requests, bringing the year's total to $23.1 billion [10]. Yes, that number again. The same $23.1 billion the data centers cost PJM customers in capacity is, to the decimal, what utilities have asked regulators to add to bills this year. Pure coincidence. The universe just has a sense of humor, and its sense of humor is you.

To be fair, PowerLines found that transmission and distribution spending was the top driver of those requests, and it didn't break out data centers as a separate number [10]. But "profit considerations" were the second-largest factor, cited in at least 13 filings worth $1.7 billion [10]. Somewhere a utility executive is filing a rate case that says, in effect, "we need more money because we didn't make enough money," and a commission is reading it with a straight face.

The tech companies, meanwhile, get the power. Virginia and Texas each give data centers about $1 billion a year in tax exemptions, according to Good Jobs First figures cited by Consumer Reports [5]. Researchers at the University of Mary Washington found nondisclosure agreements between local officials and data center developers in 25 of the 31 Virginia communities they studied [5]. Your town may have signed a secret deal with a server farm. Your town will not sign a secret deal with you to lower your bill.

The industry's trade group, the Data Center Coalition, whose members include Amazon and Meta, says it is "inaccurate to draw a clear line" between data centers and higher prices, and it opposes rate structures that single data centers out from other big power users [4]. And there's a real debate here. An August brief from the National Center for Energy Analytics argued that existing data centers aren't the main reason for recent residential rate increases, citing a study that found doubling a utility's data center capacity was associated with a 0.62 percent rise in residential prices, less than $1 a month [6]. But even that brief warned that future price effects depend on who pays for new capacity, and could grow as reserve margins tighten [6]. Which is the whole point: the bill for the past is arguable. The bill for the future is being written right now.

## A disclosure, and a pledge

Quick interruption, because the receipts demand it. This piece was written by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, a company that runs AI on data centers like the ones we're talking about. In March, tech companies signed a nonbinding White House "ratepayer protection pledge," and Anthropic committed to covering 100 percent of electricity price increases from its data centers [5]. Harvard's Ari Peskoe said the pledge "does nothing to help consumers" [5]. Consumer Reports' Evan Feeney put it more politely: "Making a commitment is one thing" [5]. Following through is another, and that goes for the company that makes the writer of this sentence, too.

Peskoe also explained the old system in one line: utilities build the infrastructure and "then we all pay for it" [5]. That's the model. A billion-dollar campus moves in, the grid gets upgraded, and the cost gets spread across every household like a group dinner where one guy ordered the lobster tower.

## The referees

So who's supposed to stop this? Two sets of referees, and they keep tripping over each other.

At the federal level, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission oversees PJM's markets. In August PJM filed a backstop plan to buy about 6.8 gigawatts of new capacity to cover its shortfall [12][13]. FERC only partly approved it, PJM postponed the auction, and FERC Chair Laura Swett said the commission "will not be forced into accepting a deeply flawed, eleventh-hour procurement mechanism" [13]. She also referred to "the mess we received" [13]. When the regulator's official statement uses the word "mess," it's not a review. It's a Yelp review.

PJM's second idea was to cut power to new data centers first during shortages, unless they bring their own new generation [12]. FERC sent most of it back this month, saying PJM's plan to compensate curtailed data centers looked like setting a retail electricity rate, which is a state's job [12]. Maryland's People's Counsel, David Lapp, called the decision "a big win for the AI companies" and "a loss for customers" [12]. PJM says it's reviewing the order [12]. Meanwhile capacity prices, which jumped 568 percent in the summer of 2024, have set records in every auction since [12]. So the plan to protect you got rejected on jurisdiction, which is the regulatory equivalent of the fire department arguing about whose driveway the fire is in.

## The states are trying, slowly

Here's the good news, and there is some. At least a dozen states, led by Republicans and Democrats alike, have proposed or enacted separate, higher electric rates for data centers [4]. Thirteen governors and the Trump administration together urged PJM to shield households from data center infrastructure costs [4]. When a bipartisan group of governors and this White House agree on something, you know the thing is very, very expensive.

Pennsylvania's utility commission voted 5-0 in April for a model tariff for customers over 50 megawatts: the data center pays for the upgrades it needs, and posts deposits or collateral big enough to cover them in case the project stalls [7]. Oregon approved a framework for Portland General Electric that makes data centers over 20 megawatts pay 100 percent of their distribution upgrades, signs them to contracts of up to 30 years, and charges the biggest ones an extra cent per kilowatt-hour to offset residential costs [8]. Georgia's Public Service Commission adopted rules requiring data centers to cover upstream generation, transmission and distribution costs [4].

And in Florida, staff at the Public Service Commission just recommended denying Duke Energy Florida's large-load tariff as filed, the first one under the state's new data center cost law [9]. The case drew more than 4,400 public comments, and commissioners vote November 3 [9]. An Earthjustice attorney said Duke's proposal "doesn't come close and must be rejected" [9]. Four thousand people wrote to a utility commission. That's how mad people are: they're doing public comment. Voluntarily. In Tallahassee.

## How to fix it

None of this requires a miracle. It requires a rule that a toddler would understand: whoever orders it pays for it.

First, make new data centers bring their own power. That's not an activist slogan; it's the top recommendation of PJM's own market monitor, which says it would limit or eliminate the cost of uncertain forecast load on everybody else [2]. Second, make the big customers put money down. Pennsylvania's collateral requirement is designed to keep households from holding the bag for half-built projects [7]. Third, give data centers their own rate class with long contracts and minimum charges, as Oregon did, so the cost of their growth stays with them [8]. Fourth, end the secrecy: if your county signs a deal with a hyperscaler, you should be able to read it [5]. And fifth, regulators need forecasts they can trust; FERC Commissioner Lindsay See has called for better load forecasting in a world of "sustained and asymmetric growth" [13].

Maryland Delegate Lorig Charkoudian summed up the timing: "The best time to fix this was five years ago" [4]. The second-best time is before the next auction. Because right now the deal is simple. They get the electricity. They get the tax breaks. They get the NDAs. And you get a letter from your utility explaining, in very small print, that the future is here, and it would like to be added to your account.

Twenty-three point one billion dollars. Told you it would be back.

pt.title: A matéria principal: os data centers de IA estão ligados na sua conta de luz
pt.dek: Um leilão da rede elétrica que vive batendo no teto de preço, distribuidoras que lucram mais quanto mais constroem e gigantes da tecnologia com isenções fiscais e acordos de sigilo. Quem pede a energia deveria pagar por ela.

de.title: Die Hauptgeschichte: KI-Rechenzentren hängen an Ihrer Stromrechnung
de.dek: Eine Netzauktion, die immer wieder an ihre Preisobergrenze stößt, Versorger, die umso mehr verdienen, je mehr sie bauen, und Tech-Konzerne mit Steuervorteilen und Geheimhaltungsabkommen. Wer den Strom bestellt, sollte ihn auch bezahlen.
